title: Name it first
hookLine: the Buddha names suffering first, the way a doctor names an illness (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
carry: stand next to it and look

cards: "It's making a noise." "What kind of noise?" "A bad one."
"When does it happen?" "I don't know, sometimes." A mechanic can't do a thing with that.
A grinding when you brake, a click when you turn left: once the noise has a plain name, the work can start. It's easy to treat our own troubles the other way round.
We fix, we distract, we explain, and we never quite say what the noise is. The Buddha's first teaching starts somewhere else. It starts by naming.

teach.b: First, a plain list. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha's first teaching lays out four noble truths, and the first is suffering, dukkha. He doesn't describe it with drama.
He lists it: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering.

teach.h: EVEN NOT GETTING WHAT YOU WANT.
teach.b: So are being joined with what you dislike, being parted from what you love, and not getting what you want. Second, look at that last one. Not getting what you want sits on the same list as death, without ranking.
A canceled plan and a funeral can both find a place there.
Third, the first task is to understand it. In the same teaching, each truth comes with its own job. Suffering is to be fully understood.
Its origin is to be let go. Its ending is to be realized. The path is to be developed.
So the first job the Buddha gives suffering isn't fix it, escape it or explain it away. It's understand it, all the way through.
Teachers sometimes use a picture for this: a good doctor names the illness before writing the prescription.
A name is a small thing, but it changes where you stand. When the trouble is a fog, you're inside it.
When it has a plain name, aging, illness, being parted from someone, not getting what I wanted, you can stand next to it and look. The cause, the ending and the path all come later.
In the Buddha's order, naming comes first.

how: Buddhists learn the four noble truths as the heart of the Buddha's first teaching, and some meditation teachers begin by asking students to notice and name their experience plainly before trying to change it.

o: the deep grief that comes only with a great loss
suffering, from death to not getting what you want
a feeling of guilt over wrongs you have done

games.q: the four truths' tasks — tap the pairs.

s: the first truth's list leaves out not getting what you want
not getting what you want is on the same list as death.
the first job the Buddha gives suffering is to understand it
suffering is to be fully understood; the cause, ending and path have their own tasks.
the Buddha describes suffering with dramatic images in the first truth
he gives a plain list: birth, aging, illness, death, and more.

games.q: you're listening to the Buddha's first teaching. something hurts. what's the first task he gives you with it?
o: escape it as fast as you can
games.why: in the first teaching, suffering is to be fully understood. letting go, realizing and developing are the tasks of the other three truths.

practice: Find one pain you're carrying right now, in the body, in a relationship, or a small frustration from this morning, and name it plainly, the way the old list does: this is worry about money; this is missing my brother; this is a sore back.
No because, no should, no story; if the story starts, come back to the plain name. Then sit beside it the way you'd sit beside a friend on a bench, close but not inside their trouble.

wordCard.voice: Dukkha, the Buddha's word for suffering, from birth and aging to not getting what you want, named plainly so it can be understood. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: noble truth, the name for each of the four in the Buddha's first teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: stand next to it and look. A plain name comes before any fix. Day seven hundred, done.
